newsitem.title: UK: FORECAST - British firms frown on EU social code.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST - British firms frown on EU social code.

text.p: Signing up for the European Social Chapter is expected to have a neutral to negative effect on prospects for small and medium-sized British companies, according to a Reuters survey published on Tuesday.

Of the 16 members of the London Stock Exchange's Alternative Investment Market (AIM) who responded to the survey, four said the impact of the European Union's (EU) social chapter on their business would be very negative and five said it would be fairly negative.
Only one contributor said the social chapter, which Britain's Labour government is keen to join, would have a fairly positive impact, while six said it would have no impact at all.

Another respondent, who declined to be named, said his company already worked within the rules of the social chapter and it would make no difference. But he said he could envisage problems for other firms.
Reuters contacted around 100 AIM firms between May 19 and 21, asking for their views on the social chapter and a proposed minimum wage for Britain.

The findings from the smaller firms are broadly in line with a poll of blue-chip companies conducted by Reuters just before the May 1 election, which brought the Labour party to power with a sweeping majority.

In that survey of FTSE-100 finance directors, 10 out of 20 respondents said the social chapter would have neither a positive nor a negative impact on business, while the remaining 10 said it would be fairly negative or very negative.

Directives in the social chapter of the Maastricht Treaty so far comprise only two -- three months unpaid parental leave and the requirement that employees of multi-national firms muct be told of corporate changes through 'works councils'.
Prime Minister Tony Blair is expected to sign Britain up at the inter-governmental conference of EU ministers on June 16 and 17.
Also on the government's agenda is a pledge to introduce a national minimum wage after consultation with employers and trades unions.

Eight contributors said they expect the implementation of a minimum wage to have no impact on their business -- principally because they already paid more than the level at which they expected it to be set.
But for those in labour-intensive industries such as health care and catering, the prospect of a minimum wage can be daunting.
Other contributors said they believed the introduction of a minimum wage would push businesses into the black market.
Five saw a very negative impact and three a fairly negative impact on their fortunes with the introduction of a minimum wage.
"Fifty percent of our costs are labour costs. We would have to go back to our customers to redress the balance. But inevitably we would lose business," said a spokesman for a health care company.
Forecasts in the survey for the level of the expected minimum wage ranged from 2.50 pounds ($4.09) to 5.50 pounds. The median of 14 predictions was 3.88 pounds.
The forecasts ranged from zero to four pounds with the median of 13 at three pounds.
